title: A Permission Is Not A Path
subtitle: Module 08 — Service identity, the two data planes, and how a Pod actually gets its address

meta.note: Timing comes from the synthesised audio. estSeconds is a planning estimate only. Content authority: assets/content.js unit u8.

beats.title: You are here
beats.narration: Segment eight of the spine: CNI. A container exists on a node and it has no address yet. This module is how it gets one. Why Service identity is a different problem with a different owner, and what to check when a name resolves but nothing answers.

visual.spec: REUSE spineLocator with segment eight lit.

beats.title: Three owners, not one network
beats.narration: Pod reachability and Service identity are two problems, and three components share them. CNI makes Pods reachable — it gives them addresses and routes. EndpointSlices record which backends are ready. kube-proxy programs each node so traffic to a Service address reaches one of those backends. An eBPF data plane can replace kube-proxy entirely. Three responsibilities, three failure modes, three sets of logs.

visual.spec: NEW. Three labelled owners across the stage, each with what it owns and how it fails: CNI (Pod address and routes → no address, ContainerCreating), EndpointSlice (which backends are ready → empty slice, no backends), kube-proxy or eBPF (Service address to backend → rules not programmed, connection times out). Each owner's failure text is the point of the beat — give it the same weight as the owner name, not a footnote.

beats.title: Readiness is the gate
beats.narration: What puts a Pod's address into an EndpointSlice is readiness. Not that the Pod exists. Not that it is Running. Readiness, and nothing else. That is the mechanical reason a readiness probe controls traffic. It changes EndpointSlice membership, and every data plane reads that membership. The probe never touches the network. It changes a list.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's Endpoints. Extend it: three Pods, one not ready. Show the ready gate admitting two addresses into the EndpointSlice and holding the third out. Then flip the third to ready and let its address appear in the slice, and only then let traffic reach it. Make the causal order visible — list first, traffic second.

beats.title: When the Service steps out
beats.narration: Setting clusterIP to None changes the shape of the answer. A headless Service hands the client the list of Pod addresses and steps out of the path. That is what per-Pod StatefulSet DNS depends on. It also means you get no load balancing at all. The client picks, and most clients pick the first address they are given.

visual.spec: NEW. Two queries side by side against the same backends. Left, a normal ClusterIP: one virtual address returned, traffic passes through the data plane, spread across backends. Right, clusterIP None: the full list of Pod addresses returned to the client, no data plane in the path, and the client connecting to the first entry every time. Label the right side with what it enables (stable per-Pod names) and what it costs (no balancing).

beats.title: A permission is not a path
beats.narration: A NetworkPolicy that allows traffic from another namespace has proven one thing: the traffic is permitted. It has not proven the traffic can arrive. A policy is a permission, not a path. It creates no routes. And if your CNI plugin does not implement NetworkPolicy, the object is accepted and then silently ignored. Allowed and unenforced look identical from the API.

visual.spec: NEW. A NetworkPolicy object drawn as a permit stamp, not a pipe. Show it granting permission while the route underneath is missing — traffic still fails, and the policy is still green. Then the worse case: a plugin with no NetworkPolicy support. The API accepts the object, nothing enforces it, and the cluster looks protected while being open. Draw the accepted-but-ignored state explicitly; it is the beat.

beats.title: Implementations, not APIs
beats.narration: iptables, IPVS, nftables and eBPF are implementations, not APIs. The Service object does not change when the backend does. Your manifests are identical across all four. That means the data plane is a swappable operational decision. It also means the Service API tells you nothing about what is actually forwarding your packets.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's DataPlane. Extend it: one unchanged Service manifest at the top feeding four interchangeable implementations below — iptables, IPVS, nftables, eBPF. Swap the implementation underneath while the manifest stays visibly identical. Do not rank them here; that is the next beat.

beats.title: Past the O(1) slogan
beats.narration: Someone will say IPVS is order one and iptables is order N, so IPVS is always faster. The slogan is right about lookup and incomplete as a recommendation. Rule update cost matters when endpoints churn. So does locality, kernel version, and the semantics each one gives you. Current clusters may well be running nftables. Naming those axes is what shows you have operated these rather than read a comparison table.

visual.spec: NEW. Start with the slogan as a two-row comparison, then expand it into a multi-axis table the slogan omits: lookup cost, rule update cost under churn, locality, kernel version, semantics. Show the naive comparison shrinking into one column of a wider table. Every axis label must be legible — this beat is the correction, so the added axes carry it.

beats.title: The requirement does not go away
beats.narration: A related claim: that an eBPF data plane removes connection tracking. Separate the implementation from the requirement. Stateful flow tracking is still needed, because something has to remember which connection a returning packet belongs to. What changes is where that state lives. It moves out of the netfilter table and into BPF maps.

visual.spec: NEW. The requirement drawn once, in the centre and unchanged: 'remember which flow this packet belongs to'. Two implementations beneath it holding the same state — netfilter conntrack table, and BPF maps. Animate the state moving from one to the other while the requirement above stays fixed. The fixed requirement is the argument.

beats.title: A program, not a service
beats.narration: A CNI plugin is a program, not a service. The runtime sets CNI_COMMAND in the environment, writes JSON configuration to the plugin's standard input, and reads a JSON result from its standard output. Then the plugin exits. It runs in the host network domain, not inside the container. Products like Calico and Cilium also run a node agent, and that agent is not the plugin.

visual.spec: REUSE the pilot's CniExec, which already draws the exec contract. Extend it: show the plugin as a short-lived process that starts, is handed CNI_COMMAND plus stdin config, returns JSON on stdout, and exits. Beside it, a long-running node agent drawn as a separate process the short-lived binary talks to. The distinction between the two is the beat — do not merge them.

beats.title: The kubelet does not call it
beats.narration: The kubelet does not call the plugin. It asks the runtime for a sandbox over CRI. The runtime creates the network namespace, reads the CNI configuration from disk, and execs the plugin chain against that namespace. So a network setup failure lives in the runtime's logs, not the kubelet's. Blaming the kubelet sends you to the wrong file.

visual.spec: NEW. The real call chain as a sequence: kubelet → CRI → runtime → creates netns → reads CNI config from disk → execs plugin chain. Draw the imagined shortcut from kubelet straight to the plugin and strike it through. Tag each hop with the log you would read if it failed there, and make the runtime's log visually prominent, since that is the one people skip.

beats.title: Where the address comes from
beats.narration: The address itself comes from somewhere else again. The main plugin delegates allocation to an IPAM plugin. That plugin receives the full configuration and returns an address, a gateway and routes. The main plugin then applies them to the interface. Allocation is delegated so that every interface plugin does not reimplement it.

visual.spec: NEW. A real nested block, not a footnote: the main plugin receives the ADD, and inside it a clearly nested IPAM call that returns address, gateway and routes. The main plugin then applies those to the interface. Render the nesting as genuine containment at full type scale — a previous cut put this detail at 14px grey against an edge and it was the point of the beat.

beats.title: It resolves, nothing answers
beats.narration: DNS resolves and the ClusterIP times out. Trace it in order. Check the Service ports and its EndpointSlices — are there ready backends at all. Test a ready Pod address directly, which splits Service from Pod. Inspect the data-plane programming: kube-proxy rules or BPF maps, and conntrack. Verify routing, MTU and NetworkPolicy. Finally confirm the target is listening on that port.

visual.spec: NEW. An ordered trace, each step lighting as named, with the check beside it and what a failure there would prove. Step two — testing a Pod address directly — should be visually emphasised as the split point, because it is the step that divides a Service problem from a Pod problem. Lay it out as rows that wrap; do not clip the longer checks.

beats.title: Back to the spine
beats.narration: Segment eight, then. A failure here has two signatures. Either the name resolves and nothing answers, or the Pod never got an address at all. Those are different layers with different owners, and the fastest question is which of the two you are in. The next segment is the one that turned a name into an address. That is module nine.
